ask_first: What triggers or worsens the dizziness?
Is the dizziness associated with position changes?
Are there any associated symptoms (e.g. nausea, hearing loss, chest pain)?

ask.changes_what: Determines which bedside exam follows: HINTS for continuous spontaneous, Dix-Hallpike for triggered episodic, orthostatic vitals for standing-triggered, ECG/monitoring for spontaneous episodic.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use a reassuring timing/trigger pattern alone to exclude stroke in patients with vascular risk factors, new headache/neck pain, or any brainstem symptom; obtain the targeted examination.
ask.escalation_warning: Acute continuous dizziness with any of diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, limb ataxia, new deafness or inability to walk unaided is a stroke pathway until proven otherwise; up to 20% of early DWI-MRI are false negative.

evidence.citation: Herr RD, Zun L, Mathews JJ. A directed approach to the dizzy patient. Ann Emerg Med. 1989;18(6):664-672.
evidence.population: 125 ED patients with dizziness evaluated with a standardized 66-item history/exam/lab protocol
evidence.quote: The best predictors, either older age, lack of vertigo, or neurologic deficit, could identify 86% of "serious" dizziness with 42% specificity.
evidence.reference_standard: Emergency physician diagnosis modified by 1-month follow-up using predefined diagnostic criteria
evidence.target_condition: 'Serious' cause of dizziness (stroke/TIA, arrhythmia, medication, seizure, other requiring admission) - composite predictor: older age OR lack of vertigo OR neurologic deficit

ask.how: Instead of asking 'what kind of dizziness', ask: Is it there now continuously or does it come in discrete episodes? How long do episodes last (seconds, minutes, hours)? Is it brought on only by a trigger (head/position change, standing) or does it arise spontaneously? Then ask about diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, new hearing loss, headache or neck pain.
ask.negative_finding: A clear positional trigger with seconds-long episodes and no neurologic symptoms makes central causes unlikely, but isolated dizziness can still be a vertebrobasilar stroke.
ask.pitfalls: Symptom-quality descriptors (vertigo vs lightheadedness) are unreliable: 52% of ED patients changed their descriptor on retest after ~6 minutes, so do not triage on 'type'. Do not confuse 'worse with movement' (most vestibular causes) with 'only occurs with movement' (true trigger).
ask.positive_finding: Continuous acute vestibular syndrome demands HINTS-type eye examination for stroke; triggered brief episodes point to BPPV or orthostatic hypotension (test with Dix-Hallpike or orthostatic vitals); spontaneous episodes lasting minutes-hours suggest TIA, Meniere or arrhythmia. Any associated brainstem symptom raises stroke probability.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; screen for red-flag neurologic symptoms before deciding on examination pathway.
ask.rationale: Clarifying timing and triggers will direct the next best bedside test and help distinguish between central, peripheral, and hemodynamic causes.
ask.title: Timing and triggers (TiTrATE: episodic vs continuous, triggered vs spontaneous) rather than symptom quality; associated diplopia/dysarthria/dysphagia/hearing loss

ask.changes_what: Positive: hold/adjust the culprit, check orthostatic vitals, ECG, creatinine and electrolytes; negative: pursue arrhythmic, structural, vasovagal or infectious causes.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not accept a medication explanation as final in patients with exertional syncope, syncope while supine, palpitations preceding syncope, known structural heart disease or an abnormal ECG.
ask.escalation_warning: Bradycardia or high-grade AV block, QT prolongation, symptomatic hypotension with AKI, or opioid/sedative toxicity with reduced consciousness need monitored care and antidote/withdrawal decisions.
ask.how: Reconcile every drug (prescribed, OTC, herbal, recreational) against the pharmacy list: antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers, PDE5 inhibitors, rate-slowing agents (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCB, digoxin), QT-prolonging drugs, sedatives/opioids, psychotropics, insulin/sulfonylureas, NSAIDs/ACEi/ARB/SGLT2i. Note start dates, dose changes and timing of the last dose versus the event.
ask.negative_finding: No culprit drug or no temporal relationship lowers the probability of medication effect but does not exclude intrinsic cardiac or neurological causes.
ask.pitfalls: Patients omit over-the-counter, recreational and 'as needed' drugs; drug effects are amplified by age, renal impairment, volume depletion and drug-drug interactions, so a long-standing drug can still be the cause after a change elsewhere. Attributing syncope to drugs without ECG review can miss conduction disease unmasked by the drug.
ask.positive_finding: A new or up-titrated vasoactive, rate-slowing, sedative or diuretic drug (or an intercurrent illness reducing intake/clearance) temporally linked to the event supports drug-induced orthostatic hypotension, bradyarrhythmia, hypovolemia/AKI or delirium.
ask.prerequisites: Access to an accurate medication list (pharmacy fill data, carer, containers); ask specifically about new drugs and dose escalations within the past 2-4 weeks.
ask.rationale: Recent changes or doses of antihypertensives or sedatives could explain dizziness and guide immediate medication adjustments.
ask.title: Antihypertensive / sedative / new-medication review (timing of last doses)

ask.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant volume loss - IV access, fluid/blood, search for bleeding source; negative: does not exclude moderate haemorrhage, use labs/other findings.
ask.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is already hypotensive, in shock, or with suspected unstable spine/pelvic injury.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing in patients who are hypotensive supine, obtunded, or at high fall risk; do not apply the volunteer-derived numbers uncritically to elderly patients on antihypertensives, beta-blockers or with autonomic neuropathy.
ask.escalation_warning: Inability to stand because of dizziness in a patient with suspected bleeding indicates large-volume loss: obtain large-bore access, type and crossmatch, and escalate immediately.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled RCE analysis of postural vital-sign studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (before vs after)
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolaemia from LARGE acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - finding: severe postural dizziness (preventing upright vitals) OR postural pulse increment >=30/min

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled RCE analysis of postural vital-sign studies)
evidence.quote: The presence of either finding has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (before vs after)
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolaemia from MODERATE acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - finding: severe postural dizziness OR postural pulse increment >=30/min

ask.how: After supine vitals, stand the patient (with assistance) and ask about dizziness while measuring pulse and BP at about 1 minute. 'Severe' means dizziness so marked the patient cannot stay standing long enough for upright vitals or nearly faints; record it as a positive finding in its own right, together with any pulse increment of 30/min or more.
ask.negative_finding: Absence is reassuring only against large blood loss (sensitivity 0.97); after moderate (450-630 mL) loss the finding is usually absent (sensitivity 0.22), so a negative test does not exclude clinically important haemorrhage.
ask.pitfalls: Mild postural dizziness has no proven diagnostic value; supine tachycardia or hypotension is often absent even after 1 L loss. Evidence comes from healthy volunteers after phlebotomy, not from elderly or medicated ED patients, in whom baseline orthostatic symptoms are common.
ask.positive_finding: Severe postural dizziness (or a postural pulse increment >=30/min) is highly specific (0.98) for hypovolaemia from blood loss and is present in almost all subjects after large (630-1150 mL) blood loss.
ask.prerequisites: Supine rest for at least 2 minutes before standing; an assistant to prevent a fall. Sitting is not an adequate substitute for standing.
ask.rationale: Severe postural dizziness or inability to stand suggests significant volume loss or orthostatic hypotension, prompting urgent intervention.
ask.title: Severe postural dizziness / inability to stand for vitals

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant hypovolemia/bleeding or medication-related OH and act; negative: large blood loss unlikely, but moderate loss still possible.
examine.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is frankly hypotensive, has an unstable spine/pelvis, or cannot safely bear weight.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing measurements in a patient who is already hypotensive, too dizzy or weak to stand safely, or has an unstable spine or pelvis; a patient too dizzy to stand counts as a positive test.
examine.escalation_warning: A positive test in a patient with possible bleeding indicates large volume loss and should trigger resuscitation and source search, not observation.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.target_condition: Large acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.target_condition: Moderate acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy
evidence.quote: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent, even after up to 1150 mL of blood loss (sensitivity, 33%; 95% CI, 21%-47%, for supine hypotension)
evidence.target_condition: Blood loss up to 1150 mL - supine hypotension (comparator finding, not postural)

examine.how: Measure BP and pulse after >=2 min supine, then have the patient stand and repeat at 1 and 3 min (standing, not sitting). Record SBP fall >=20 or DBP fall >=10 mmHg, pulse rise >=30/min, and whether the patient is too dizzy to stand (count that as positive).
examine.negative_finding: A normal postural pulse response argues strongly against large blood loss (LR- about 0.03) but misses most moderate (450-630 mL) losses (sensitivity 22%). Normal orthostatics do not exclude hypovolemia from vomiting/diarrhea.
examine.pitfalls: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent even after 1 L blood loss. Beta-blockers blunt the pulse response; sitting instead of standing lowers sensitivity; mild postural dizziness alone has no proven value.
examine.positive_finding: A postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness is highly specific (98%) for blood loss and is nearly always present after large (>1 L) hemorrhage. In an older patient with syncope, an SBP fall >=20 mmHg reproducing symptoms supports orthostatic hypotension, though asymptomatic falls are common with age and medications.
examine.prerequisites: Automated or manual cuff, an assistant to steady the patient, supine rest of at least 2 minutes first.
examine.rationale: Orthostatic vitals can quickly identify orthostatic hypotension as a cause of acute dizziness.
examine.title: Orthostatic vitals: SBP drop >=20 / DBP >=10 mmHg or pulse increment >=30/min at 1-3 min standing

examine.changes_what: Central-pattern nystagmus: treat as posterior-circulation stroke; obtain MRI/stroke consult. Peripheral-pattern nystagmus alone does not rule out stroke; combine with HIT and skew (HINTS).
examine.do_not_use_when: Not applicable to episodic/triggered vertigo without spontaneous nystagmus (use Dix-Hallpike); a fixation-suppressed or absent nystagmus makes the HINTS battery uninterpretable.
examine.escalation_warning: Vertical, pure torsional or gaze-direction-changing nystagmus in acute vertigo should trigger the stroke pathway even if the patient looks well and CT is normal (early MRI-DWI misses ~15% of posterior strokes).

evidence.citation: Diagnostic accuracy of the physical examination in emergency department patients with acute vertigo or dizziness: a systematic review and meta-analysis for GRACE-3. Acad Emerg Med. 2023;30(5):552-578.
evidence.population: ED patients with acute vertigo or dizziness; 16 studies, 1366 patients
evidence.quote: pure torsional nystagmus are consistent with a central cause of vertigo, sensitivity 50.7% [95% CI 41.1%-60.2%, moderate] and specificity 98.5% [95% CI 91.7%-99.7%
evidence.target_condition: Central cause of acute vertigo/dizziness - central nystagmus type (bidirectional, vertical, direction-changing or pure torsional)

evidence.citation: Tarnutzer AA, Gold D, Wang Z, et al. Impact of clinician training background and stroke location on bedside diagnostic test accuracy in the acute vestibular syndrome - a meta-analysis. Ann Neurol. 2023;94(2):295-308.
evidence.location: Results, 'Diagnostic accuracy of bedside examination findings' (Ann Neurol 2023;94:295; PMC10524166); full values in supplementary Table 2
evidence.population: Pooled AVS cohorts (10 studies; direction-changing nystagmus assessed in 400 central and 376 peripheral patients)
evidence.quote: considerably lower for the other tests including the test of skew (27.0% [16.1-37.9]), direction-changing nystagmus on lateral-gaze test (37.3% [27.2-47.3])
evidence.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
evidence.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome - direction-changing nystagmus on lateral gaze

examine.how: With the patient looking straight ahead, observe for spontaneous nystagmus and note the direction of the fast phase; then have them follow your finger about 30 degrees to the right, left, up and down, holding each position several seconds, and record whether the fast phase reverses direction with gaze. Remove fixation if possible (penlight/ophthalmoscope cover, Frenzel lenses).
examine.negative_finding: Unidirectional horizontal(-torsional) nystagmus that obeys Alexander's law and suppresses with fixation is the expected pattern of vestibular neuritis, but a peripheral-appearing nystagmus does not exclude stroke: central nystagmus patterns are seen in only about 37-51% of central AVS.
examine.pitfalls: End-gaze physiologic nystagmus at extreme lateral gaze and drug-induced gaze-evoked nystagmus (anticonvulsants, sedatives, alcohol) are false positives; fixation can suppress peripheral nystagmus and hide it. Positional nystagmus of BPPV is triggered, transient and torsional-upbeating, not spontaneous.
examine.positive_finding: Horizontal nystagmus whose fast phase changes direction with gaze (gaze-evoked, bidirectional), predominantly vertical (up/down-beat) or pure torsional nystagmus indicates a central lesion; specificity for a central cause is about 98% in pooled ED studies and was 100% (0/25 peripheral) in Kattah's AVS cohort.
examine.prerequisites: Patient must be able to hold eccentric gaze; avoid extreme lateral gaze (physiologic end-point nystagmus). Meaningful mainly in acute vestibular syndrome with ongoing spontaneous nystagmus.
examine.rationale: Identifying central-pattern nystagmus is critical to rule out posterior circulation stroke, which requires urgent action.
examine.title: Nystagmus: direction-changing / vertical / pure torsional (central) vs unidirectional horizontal (peripheral)

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as stroke until imaged, especially if anticoagulated (urgent CT for hemorrhage). Negative in a dizzy patient: still needs HINTS/gait assessment; does not exclude stroke.
examine.contraindications: None. Do not stand a patient who is vomiting, severely ataxic or hypotensive to test gait.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never use a normal three-item screen to exclude stroke in acute vertigo, ataxia, diplopia or visual loss; posterior-circulation strokes frequently have none of the three findings.
examine.escalation_warning: New focal deficit in an anticoagulated patient is intracranial hemorrhage until proven otherwise: urgent CT and reversal pathway. Any focal deficit within the reperfusion window is time-critical.

evidence.citation: Goldstein LB, Simel DL. Is this patient having a stroke? JAMA. 2005;293(19):2391-2402.
evidence.population: Pooled studies of patients with neurologically relevant symptoms, modern neuroimaging (RCE systematic review)
evidence.quote: acute facial paresis, arm drift, or abnormal speech increases the likelihood of stroke (LR of > or =1 finding = 5.5; 95% CI, 3.3-9.1)
evidence.reference_standard: Final diagnosis after neuroimaging and laboratory tests

evidence.citation: Diagnostic accuracy of the physical examination in emergency department patients with acute vertigo or dizziness: a systematic review and meta-analysis for GRACE-3. Acad Emerg Med. 2023;30(5):552-578.
evidence.population: ED patients with acute vertigo or dizziness; 5 studies, 869 patients
evidence.quote: general neurologic examination-five studies, 869 patients, pooled sensitivity 46.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 32.3%-61.9%, moderate certainty) and specificity 92.8% (95% CI 75.7%-98.1%
evidence.target_condition: Central cause (stroke, hemorrhage, other) of acute vertigo/dizziness - general neurologic examination abnormal

evidence.citation: Diagnostic accuracy of the physical examination in emergency department patients with acute vertigo or dizziness: a systematic review and meta-analysis for GRACE-3. Acad Emerg Med. 2023;30(5):552-578.
evidence.population: ED patients with acute vertigo or dizziness; 4 studies, 893 patients
evidence.quote: limb weakness/hemiparesis-four studies, 893 patients, sensitivity 11.4% (95% CI 5.1%-23.6%, high) and specificity 98.5% (95% CI 97.1%-99.2%, high)
evidence.target_condition: Central cause of acute vertigo/dizziness - limb weakness/hemiparesis

evidence.citation: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009;40(11):3504-3510.
evidence.location: Table 1 (PAVS n=25 vs CAVS n=76), Stroke 2009;40:3504 (PMC4593511)
evidence.population: 101 consecutive high-risk AVS patients (25 peripheral, 76 central) at a stroke referral center
evidence.reference_standard: MRI (or CT) for stroke; normal MRI plus clinical follow-up for peripheral
evidence.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome (stroke or other central lesion) - any general neurologic sign including truncal ataxia

examine.how: Brief structured screen: facial symmetry on smile, pronator drift with arms held out and eyes closed for 10 s, and speech (repeat a sentence, name objects). Add gaze (ask to look left/right), visual fields by confrontation, finger-nose and heel-shin, and gait if safe, because dizzy or confused patients often lack the three classic items.
examine.negative_finding: A normal focal screen lowers stroke probability modestly overall (LR about 0.4 for absence of face/arm/speech findings) but is insensitive for posterior-circulation stroke: pooled sensitivity of the general neurologic exam in acute vertigo is under 50%, and in Kattah's AVS cohort general signs were absent in 49% of central lesions.
examine.pitfalls: Confusion, aphasia and encephalopathy from hypoglycemia, seizure or intoxication mimic focal deficits; a normal screen in a dizzy patient is falsely reassuring, so add HINTS and a gait test. Old deficits must be compared with baseline.
examine.positive_finding: Any new focal finding (facial paresis, arm drift, dysarthria/aphasia, gaze palsy, hemisensory loss, limb ataxia) strongly favours a central lesion; in dizzy patients such general neurologic signs are highly specific for a central cause (pooled specificity about 93%; limb weakness 98.5%).
examine.prerequisites: Bedside glucose; note baseline deficits, time last known well and anticoagulant use. Patient must be able to follow at least one-step commands or the screen defaults to observation of asymmetry.
examine.rationale: A focal neurological deficit would prompt immediate stroke workup and imaging.
examine.title: Focal deficit screen: facial droop, arm drift, speech (Cincinnati/NIHSS-lite)

examine.changes_what: Cannot stand/walk unaided (grade 3): treat as central; stroke work-up regardless of HINTS. Walks unaided: lowers but does not remove need for HINTS; still image if other red flags.
examine.contraindications: Do not attempt to stand a hypotensive, actively vomiting or obtunded patient; use the sitting test instead.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not stand hypotensive, vomiting or obtunded patients; interpret with caution in patients with baseline gait impairment (neuropathy, parkinsonism, prior stroke, intoxication) where inability to walk is not new.
examine.escalation_warning: New inability to stand or walk unaided with acute vertigo is a central sign until proven otherwise, even with a normal CT and a peripheral-appearing HINTS; Carmona 2023 found truncal ataxia without nystagmus in 15% of acute-vertigo patients, mostly strokes.

evidence.citation: Tarnutzer AA, Gold D, Wang Z, et al. Impact of clinician training background and stroke location on bedside diagnostic test accuracy in the acute vestibular syndrome - a meta-analysis. Ann Neurol. 2023;94(2):295-308.
evidence.population: Pooled AVS cohorts (10 study cohorts, n=800; stroke and vestibular neuritis)
evidence.quote: Severe (grade 3) gait/truncal instability had high specificity 99.2% (95% CI = 97.8-100.0) but low sensitivity 35.8% (95% CI = 5.2-66.5).
evidence.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
evidence.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome (stroke or other central lesion) - severe (grade 3) gait/truncal instability

evidence.citation: Tarnutzer AA, Gold D, Wang Z, et al. Impact of clinician training background and stroke location on bedside diagnostic test accuracy in the acute vestibular syndrome - a meta-analysis. Ann Neurol. 2023;94(2):295-308.
evidence.location: Results, 'Diagnostic accuracy of bedside examination findings' (Ann Neurol 2023;94:295; PMC10524166); supplementary Table 2
evidence.quote: highest for a normal hHIT (79.9% [95% CI 72.2-87.5]), grade 2 or 3 gait/truncal instability (80.8% [45.1-100.0])
evidence.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
evidence.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome - grade 2 or 3 gait/truncal instability

evidence.citation: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of a graded gait and truncal instability rating in acutely dizzy and ataxic patients. Cerebellum. 2024.
evidence.population: 18 studies, 1025 patients with acute vestibular syndrome (665 ischemic strokes, 306 acute unilateral vestibulopathy)
evidence.quote: Grade 2/3 GTI had moderate sensitivity (70.8% [95% confidence-interval (CI) = 59.3-82.3%]) and specificity (82.7 [71.6-93.8%]) for predicting a central cause
evidence.target_condition: Central cause of acute prolonged vertigo/imbalance - grade 2/3 graded gait/truncal instability (GTI)

evidence.citation: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of a graded gait and truncal instability rating in acutely dizzy and ataxic patients. Cerebellum. 2024.
evidence.quote: grade 3 GTI had a lower sensitivity (44.0% [34.3-53.7%] and higher specificity (99.1% [98.0-100.0%]).
evidence.target_condition: Central cause of acute prolonged vertigo/imbalance - grade 3 GTI (cannot stand/walk unaided)

evidence.citation: Kattah JC, Martinez C, Zalazar G, Batuecas A, Lemos J, Carmona S. Role of incubitus truncal ataxia, and equivalent standing grade 3 ataxia in the diagnosis of central acute vestibular syndrome. J Neurol Sci. 2022;441:120374.
evidence.population: 52 prospectively studied AVS patients (stroke and vestibular neuritis)
evidence.quote: grade 2-3 ataxia to differentiate patients with vestibular neuritis from patients with stroke resulted in a 92% sensitivity (95% CI 79-100%), a 67% specificity
evidence.target_condition: AICA/PICA-territory stroke vs vestibular neuritis - grade 2-3 truncal ataxia (including inability to sit still as substitute)

evidence.citation: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009;40(11):3504-3510.
evidence.population: 101 consecutive high-risk AVS patients (69 ischemic strokes vs 25 peripheral) at a stroke referral center
evidence.reference_standard: MRI (or CT) for stroke; normal MRI plus clinical follow-up for peripheral
evidence.target_condition: Ischemic stroke in AVS - severe truncal ataxia (cannot sit unassisted)

examine.how: With an assistant ready, ask the patient to sit unsupported, then stand, then walk a few metres. Grade truncal/gait instability: 0 = normal; 1 = mild sway but walks unaided; 2 = walks only with support/one-sided assistance; 3 = cannot stand or walk even with support (or cannot sit without arm support). If the patient cannot get up, note whether they can sit still unassisted.
examine.negative_finding: Walking unaided does not exclude posterior-circulation stroke: grade 3 instability is present in only about 36-44% of central AVS, so a patient who can walk still needs HINTS and imaging assessment when indicated.
examine.pitfalls: Peripheral vestibular neuritis causes unsteadiness (grade 1-2) that is easily over-called, especially in the elderly, the intoxicated or those with prior neuropathy; sedatives, Wernicke encephalopathy and alcohol withdrawal also produce ataxia. Grading systems differ (Lee 2006 vs Moon 2009), which changes sensitivity.
examine.positive_finding: Grade 3 instability (cannot stand or walk unaided) in acute vertigo is almost exclusively central - pooled specificity about 99% (LR+ high), and 0/25 peripheral patients in Kattah 2009. Grade 2-3 instability is more sensitive (71-81% pooled) but less specific (83%).
examine.prerequisites: Adequate blood pressure and no orthostatic symptoms; assistant present for fall prevention. Compare with baseline mobility in elderly or frail patients.
examine.rationale: Inability to stand or walk unaided is a strong marker for central causes and would escalate to stroke pathway regardless of other findings.
examine.title: Ability to stand and walk unaided (truncal ataxia grade; inability = central marker)

Recent changes or doses of antihypertensives or sedatives could explain dizziness and guide immediate medication adjustments.
Severe postural dizziness or inability to stand suggests significant volume loss or orthostatic hypotension, prompting urgent intervention.

Identifying central-pattern nystagmus is critical to rule out posterior circulation stroke, which requires urgent action.
A focal neurological deficit would prompt immediate stroke workup and imaging.
